planting.note: Set out nursery transplants after frost danger passes into sharply drained, sandy or gritty soil, since this Canary Islands native rots quickly in wet winter ground.

directions: This Canary Islands subshrub forms a broad rosette of large, leathery, silvery-green leaves beneath wiry stems topped with dense clusters of papery purple-blue calyces that hold their color for months, long after the small true flowers inside them fade. It is a mainstay of coastal Southern California and other Mediterranean-climate landscapes, where it thrives in lean, fast-draining soil with minimal irrigation once roots are established. Shear off spent flower stems at the base to tidy the clump and encourage repeat flushes through the warm season. It tolerates salt spray and wind exceptionally well, making it a dependable choice for seaside gardens where few other flowering perennials perform.

planting.note: Plant in a lean, gritty rock-garden or trough mix with sharp drainage, since this low mat-former dislikes rich or consistently damp soil.

directions: Native to coastal salt meadows and dry steppe from Europe into central Asia, this diminutive sea lavender forms a tight rosette of narrow, leathery leaves that hugs the ground while wiry, branched flower stems rise just a few inches to carry a haze of tiny lavender-pink blooms in summer. It is an excellent choice for an alpine trough, scree bed, or the front of a well-drained rock garden where its fine texture and salt tolerance stand out against coarser plants. Avoid rich garden soil and overhead watering, both of which encourage rot in this otherwise tough, drought- and salt-tolerant little perennial. Established clumps need almost no maintenance beyond an occasional trim of old flower stems.

planting.note: Set container-grown plants into humus-rich, acidic soil in dappled shade and keep evenly moist through the first growing season.

directions: This New Zealand native is one of the most variable Gaultheria species in cultivation, ranging from a low, wiry groundcover in exposed alpine sites to a small upright shrub in sheltered forest margins, with small leathery leaves and tiny urn-shaped white or pink-tinged flowers in late spring. The flowers give way to translucent white, pink, or red berries that persist into winter and are an important food source for native birds. Grow in acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and light shade, mimicking the forest-edge conditions of its native range, and avoid limy or waterlogged ground. It is best suited to native-plant and woodland gardens rather than formal borders, since named, size-consistent selections are rarely available in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted layers into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil in a shaded alpine bed and keep consistently moist but never waterlogged.

directions: Collected from high-elevation scree and alpine turf across the Himalaya, this tiny creeping shrublet forms a dense, wiry mat of minute bristly leaves that roots as it spreads, making it a choice specimen for a shaded trough or peat bed. In spring it bears small, nodding, bell-shaped white to pink flowers, followed later in the season by its most distinctive feature, unusual china-blue berries that stand out sharply against the dark foliage. It demands cool roots, acidic humus-rich soil, and protection from hot afternoon sun, conditions best replicated in a shaded rock garden, alpine house, or peat bed rather than a conventional border. Top-dress annually with leaf mold to maintain the cool, moisture-retentive soil this high-altitude species expects.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in a sheltered sunny spot, since this hebe resents both winter wet and hard freezes.

directions: Native to New Zealand's mountain forests and scrub, this compact hebe carries tiny, tightly packed, box-like leaves on a dense, rounded shrub, giving it an almost dwarf-conifer appearance even without pruning. Clusters of small white flowers appear at the branch tips in early summer, drawing bees, though the plant is grown chiefly for its neat year-round foliage structure. Grow in sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade and shelter it from drying winter winds, which can scorch the foliage in colder parts of its hardiness range. Light shearing after flowering keeps the naturally tidy habit even denser, and it combines well with other compact evergreens in a mixed foundation planting or low hedge.
